Although this temperature is much higher than that of LNG, ethane is still a cryogenic fluid; its handling requires careful selection of materials, pressure control, thermal protection, etc. Current Jet A fueling networks cannot support these conditions, and thus require upgraded insulated piping, cryogenic-rated transfer equipment, enhanced leak prevention systems, and revised inspection and emergency protocols. Ground personnel would also need specialized training in managing the unique hazards of cold ethane handling, namely the formation of a vapor cloud and embrittlement of machinery. LE can be delivered to an airport via truck or pipeline and stored either directly or after on-site liquefaction. To keep LE in liquefied state, airports would have to use vacuum-insulated, double- walled cryogenic tanks designed for ethane’s comparatively high vapor pressure w.r.t jet fuel. These tanks are typically manufactured as horizontal or vertical cylinders, with capacities ranging from tens to thousands of cubic meters, depending on operational scale. As with other cryogenic fuels, minimizing the surface area relative to the stored volume helps reduce boil-off gas generation. Although spherical pressure vessels provide the best geometry for limiting thermal ingress, because of their cost and manufacturing complexity they are uncommon for LE applications. Concepts for fuel transfer may also be borrowed from the ethane shipping industry. For instance, an aircraft could be connected directly using a fixed cryogenic loading arm, like those used at marine ethane terminals. Such systems maintain stable insulation, allow controlled boil-off gas recovery, and would reduce the number of refuelers circulating on the apron. Before such equipment could be employed in an aviation context, significant certification efforts would be necessary. A more flexible alternative is the use of LE ISO containers: standard cryogenic tank modules in 20- or 40-foot format equipped with pumps and monitoring systems. These LE ISO containers are ready for use as refuelers and could minimize the need for dedicated ethane tanker trucks. No cryogenic ethane systems are used in civil aviation facilities, but similar technologies have been extensively deployed in marine transport, the petrochemical industry, and the heavy-duty distribution of cryogens. Their reliability in operations demonstrates possible applicability for LE within forthcoming aircraft fueling infrastructure, provided adequate testing, engineering optimization, and aviation safety approval.
